statements.text: It warns that international researchers may increasingly choose to work in countries like Canada or the U.K. due to visa uncertainty. We know that nearly 50 percent of noncitizen AI Ph.D.s face immigration challenges, and many are unsure if they will even remain here. [...] So, Ms. Toner, if we continue to make it harder for top talent to stay, what are the strategic risks to U.S. innovation and our ability to protect those innovations through trade secrets?
statements.context: House committee hearing titled 'Protecting Our Edge: Trade Secrets and the Global AI Arms Race,' where a member questions an expert witness.

statements.text: We cannot protect our edge in AI and cybersecurity, actually, without investing in the people and the institutions that are building the edge. I'm talking about colleges and universities that feel like they are under attack—the faculty, the curriculum, the prospective students, and the students that are there right now.

statements.text: Today, we will examine the Fiscal Year '26 budget request for BIS and discuss the role of export controls within the larger national security objective of ensuring U.S. leadership in the global AI race.
statements.context: Opening statement at a House Foreign Affairs Committee hearing on the Bureau of Industry and Security FY 2026 budget, focused on export controls and the AI competition with China.

statements.text: Thank you, Mr. Chair. And I'm so glad that we're still having these conversations. Great questions. [...] So would you commit right now that no advanced U.S. AI chips would be exported to the UAE or Saudi Arabia until those governments sign a binding security and monitoring agreement?
statements.context: House hearing on the BIS FY2026 budget, during a Q&A exchange with the Under Secretary about Gulf AI chip deals and export-control enforcement.
